title: Language and Testimony in Classical Indian Philosophy

summaries.example: Imagine hearing someone say, “The school is on the river.” A school building cannot sit on moving water, so you may understand the speaker to mean that it is beside the river. Indian thinkers used examples like this to explain secondary meaning: when the first meaning does not fit, listeners look for a related meaning that makes sense.
summaries.summary: Classical Indian philosophers and grammarians explored language in many ways. Early Vedic writings sometimes described speech as divine and powerful in rituals. Later thinkers asked whether the Vedas were made by people, created by a god, or eternal and authorless. They also studied how words get meanings, whether words point to individual things or shared kinds, and how words form sentences. Some schools believed language can provide reliable knowledge, while others stressed that language may not show reality exactly. Their disagreements were connected to their larger goals, such as grammar, logic, scripture, poetry, or spiritual practice.
key_ideas: Indian philosophers asked whether language is divine, human, eternal, changing, or connected to reality.
Different schools disagreed about what words mean and how sentences communicate.
Some thinkers treated the Vedas as eternal and not made by humans; others gave different reasons for trusting them.
Some grammarians said a whole sentence is understood all at once, while other thinkers explained sentences by combining word meanings.
summaries.why_it_matters: Language is part of everyday life: we use it to ask, teach, promise, explain, and imagine. These Indian debates show that even a simple question like “What does this word mean?” can lead to bigger questions about truth, knowledge, religion, and reality. They also remind us that people may understand language differently because they begin with different ideas about the world.

important_terms.definition: The study of how words and sentences communicate ideas or things.
A meaning used when the first, literal meaning does not fit the situation.
The ancient collection of sacred texts called the Vedas.
Knowledge learned from a trustworthy speaker or text when other ways of knowing are not enough.
A group or kind of thing that different individual members share, such as “cowness” shared by cows.

questions_to_think_about: When a sentence sounds strange, how do you decide what the speaker meant?
Can words teach us something true about the world?
Is a sentence just a group of words, or does it have its own meaning as a whole?
Why might different communities develop different ideas about language?

summaries.example: Suppose a person says, “There is a village on the Ganges.” The literal wording seems to place the village in the river. Indian theories of secondary meaning explain why a listener may instead understand “on the bank of the Ganges.” The alternative meaning is not random: it is connected to the literal meaning and is selected because the literal interpretation does not fit the speaker’s likely intention.
summaries.summary: The entry surveys theories of language and testimony in Indian thought from Vedic texts through classical and medieval philosophical schools. Vedic traditions present speech as divine, ritually effective, and at times fundamental to the universe, while the Upaniṣadic discussion also treats the highest reality as beyond complete verbal description. Sanskrit grammarians examined permanence and change in sounds, the relation between uttered sounds and more stable linguistic units, and the status of words and sentences. Bhartṛhari made the sentence an undivided unit whose meaning is grasped in a flash, whereas many other schools analyzed sentences through relations among word-meanings. Mīmāṃsā held that the Vedas are eternal and authorless, with an innate word-meaning relation; Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika instead connected linguistic authority to God as an omniscient and trustworthy speaker. Across the traditions, theories of artha, or meaning, range from external objects to conceptual contents, and include primary, secondary, suggested, and intended meanings. The disagreements reflect different philosophical purposes rather than one shared question answered in one way.
key_ideas: Vedic and later philosophical traditions moved among several pictures of speech: divine power, a ritual instrument, a human communicative practice, and a principle connected with reality.
Mīmāṃsā defended the Vedas as eternal, authorless, and intrinsically meaningful, while Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika defended their authority through the idea of a trustworthy divine speaker.
Debates about word-meaning included whether a word primarily denotes an individual, a universal, or both together.
Most schools analyzed sentences through their parts, but Bhartṛhari argued that the sentence and its meaning are fundamentally undivided.
Theories of meaning included primary, secondary, suggested, and intended meanings, although schools differed over which functions they accepted.
The aims of each school shaped its theory: logic sought truth about reality, Mīmāṃsā interpreted scripture and duty, grammarians studied language and cognition, and poetics studied suggestion.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry shows that philosophy of language is never isolated from questions about knowledge and reality. Whether words have natural or conventional meanings, whether sentences are basic or composed, and whether scripture is authoritative all depend partly on what a tradition thinks exists and how truth can be known. Studying these debates also complicates familiar modern divisions such as sense versus reference: artha can cover objects, concepts, grammatical information, and what a hearer understands in context.

important_terms.definition: The Sanskrit term often used for what a word communicates, ranging from an external object to conceptual content; it does not map neatly onto one English term such as “reference.”
The idea that words, meanings, or scriptures exist without a human beginning and do not perish.
The claim that the Vedas have no human author; Mīmāṃsā uses this to explain their authority.
A source of knowledge gained through language, especially the testimony of a trustworthy speaker or authoritative text.
A theory associated with Bhartṛhari in which the sentence is the basic, undivided linguistic unit and its meaning appears in a single cognitive flash.
A function that supplies a related, nonliteral meaning when the primary meaning is unsuitable in context.
The view that words initially communicate meanings that are not yet connected, after which their relations produce sentence-meaning.
The view that words in a sentence communicate already-related meanings, so sentence-meaning is not added after separate word-meanings.

questions_to_think_about: If a word can refer to individuals and also to a shared class, which should count as its primary meaning?
Does a sentence acquire meaning by adding word-meanings together, or is its meaning grasped as a whole?
What makes testimony trustworthy: the words themselves, the speaker, the tradition, or the method by which they were preserved?
Can an expression be meaningful even if it does not refer to anything that exists?
How do a school’s views about reality and knowledge influence its theory of language?

summaries.example: A friend says, “The team is on fire,” after a great game. You probably do not imagine flames. You move from the primary meaning to a related meaning such as “playing extremely well.” Indian thinkers discussed a similar move when a literal meaning did not fit a context. They called this kind of move secondary meaning, and they asked how listeners know which related meaning is intended.
summaries.summary: The entry introduces a long history of Indian thinking about language, meaning, and verbal knowledge. In early Vedic materials, speech is linked with gods, ritual success, and creative power. Later traditions ask whether sacred texts are human products, divine words, or eternal and uncreated. Sanskrit grammarians study how spoken sounds, words, and sentences work. They debate whether words name particular objects, shared classes, or both. Other schools develop different accounts of meaning. Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika generally connects words with real things and explains the word-world link through convention established by God. Mīmāṃsā holds that the Vedic word-meaning relation is innate and eternal. Grammarians often focus on the concepts understood by a listener without settling whether every concept corresponds to an external object. Sentence theories also differ: some build a sentence from related word meanings, while Bhartṛhari treats the sentence as a unified whole grasped in a single act of understanding. These differences come from the schools’ wider interests in scripture, logic, grammar, spirituality, and poetry.
key_ideas: Early Vedic ideas treated speech as powerful in worship and sometimes as a divine reality.
Sanskrit grammarians debated whether words are permanent and how temporary spoken sounds can express stable words.
Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika both treated the Vedas as authoritative, but they explained that authority differently.
Some philosophers thought words mainly refer to real things; others emphasized concepts or the limits of language.
Theories of sentences disagreed about whether connected meaning is present in the words from the start or formed after separate meanings are understood.
Bhartṛhari argued that people truly understand a whole sentence at once, while grammatical parts are later analytical tools.
summaries.why_it_matters: We depend on language to learn from other people, understand rules, interpret stories, and describe the world. The Indian debates help us notice hidden choices in ordinary communication: whether meanings belong to words or contexts, whether a speaker’s intention matters, and whether language reveals reality or only our way of organizing experience. Comparing several traditions is useful because it shows that disagreement can result from different goals and starting assumptions, not simply from carelessness.

important_terms.definition: What a word communicates, such as an object, an idea, or information understood in a sentence.
A meaning communicated directly by a word in a particular use.
A related meaning chosen when the direct meaning does not make sense in context.
A claim that the Vedas have no human author and are not created like ordinary books.
Learning something through words from a speaker or text regarded as reliable.
A shared feature or class, such as the common property that makes different animals cows.
The way a sentence communicates an overall message, including how its words fit together.

questions_to_think_about: When does a figurative expression need a second meaning?
Do different people use a word because they share a convention, or because the word has a built-in connection to its meaning?
Could a text be trustworthy without having a human author?
What is gained, and what might be lost, by analyzing a sentence into smaller parts?
Why might a poet, grammarian, and logician study meaning differently?
